1415.title: The hymn that bows to everything
1415.hook: namah, namah, namah: a hymn that faces an angry god with a strung bow, and starts by bowing
1415.carry: the rudram bows to shiva in everything
1415.tomorrow: a woman judges a debate between two great teachers. whose garland wilts first?
1415.howItsDone: The Sri Rudram is chanted in Shiva temples and homes, often during abhisheka, when water, milk or other offerings are poured over the linga, and through the night of Maha Shivaratri.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nataraja read all at once: the drum and the flame, held level. Shiva's lifted foot is grace.
screen: `SHIVA'S LIFTED FOOT IS GRACE.` · `THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Namah. Namah. Namah. Said once, it's a bow, a word of homage. Said over and over in a steady chant, it becomes a rhythm you can feel in the floor. The hymn built on it faces a god who is not, at first, gentle. Rudra stands with his bow strung and an arrow ready. And the hymn doesn't run, and doesn't argue. It bows: to the arrow, to the bow, to the anger itself. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Rudram, and the night the year spent awake with Shiva.
screen: `NAMAH, NAMAH, NAMAH.` → `A GOD WITH A STRUNG BOW.` → `THE HYMN BOWS.`

segments.voice: The Rudram comes from the Yajur Veda. In paraphrase, it opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrow, and to his arms. Then it asks: make that arrow gentle; let your kind form be turned toward us. That's the first move. Fear isn't hidden or argued away. It's bowed to, and asked to soften. Then the hymn widens. It bows to Rudra in the short and the tall, the eldest and the youngest. In the trees with green hair. In the rain and in the drought, in the well and in the foam on the water. In thieves, even, and in the carpenters and the potters. Line after line, namah, until almost nothing in the world is left out of the bowing. Rudra isn't only on the mountain. He's in the crowd, the weather and the workshop. Then its companion, often chanted right after, turns the direction. Line after line, it asks: and to me, strength, food, breath, peace, long life. Bowing to everything, then asking honestly for what a person needs. The year carried that hymn into the dark, too. On Maha Shivaratri, it's chanted while water pours over the linga, through a night kept awake, often without food, until the gray light comes. That's the teaching under the hymn: Shiva isn't only on the mountain or in the temple. He is in every being, the frightening ones included. In many homes it's still chanted on Mondays, Shiva's day, as water runs over a small linga. And it trains the eye for an ordinary day: the boss who scares you, the neighbor you'd rather avoid. Namah comes first.
screen: `BOW TO THE ANGER. ASK THE ARROW TO SOFTEN.` · `NAMAH TO THE TREES, THE RAIN, THE POTTER.` · `AND TO ME: AN HONEST ASK.` · `A NIGHT KEPT AWAKE.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT OUT OF THE BOWING.`

segments.voice: Let the bow move outward, one thing per breath: your own body, the room, the people nearby, the weather outside, someone who makes you angry. If something feels too hard to bow to, bow to the hard feeling instead; if you pray, say namah softly with each one.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Rudram and Shivaratri, a hymn that bows to an angry god and then to everything. Today's word.

1416.title: The debate judged by a garland
1416.hook: a young monk walks to a great ritualist's door to argue, and the judge is the ritualist's wife
1416.carry: truth is one; the wise call it by many names
1416.tomorrow: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast. then, a knock.
1416.howItsDone: The darshanas are still studied through their root texts and commentaries in traditional schools and universities, and formal debate, shastrartha, is still held at some gatherings of scholars.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram, a hymn that bows to an angry god, then to everything. The Rudram bows to Shiva in everything.
screen: `THE RUDRAM BOWS TO EVERYTHING.` · `BOW, AND ASK IT TO SOFTEN.`

segments.voice: A young monk walks into a strange town, looking for one house. He asks the women at the well which one belongs to Mandana Mishra, the great master of the Vedic rites. The story goes that they told him: look for the house where even the parrots at the door are arguing about the Vedas. The monk is Shankara. He hasn't come to visit. He's come to debate. Today's summit sit climbs back to the schools of thought, the darshanas, through the most famous argument the tradition tells.
screen: `A MONK LOOKING FOR ONE HOUSE.` → `PARROTS ARGUING AT THE DOOR.` → `THE DEBATE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Shankara Digvijaya, a much later life of Shankara, tells it. Mandana held the view of Mimamsa: the Vedas are above all a call to act, and the rites done rightly are the point. Shankara held Vedanta: the rites prepare you, but freedom comes from knowing Brahman, the one reality. Who could judge them? Mandana's wife, Ubhaya Bharati, a famous scholar herself. She hung a fresh garland around each man's neck and said: whoever's garland wilts first has lost. The debate, the tradition says, ran for days. At last Mandana's flowers began to fade. And the story doesn't end with a sneer. Mandana became Shankara's student, and many remember him as Sureshvara, one of Shankara's great disciples. Then, the story says, Ubhaya Bharati challenged Shankara herself. That's the teaching under the story. Hinduism never settled on one school of thought. It kept its darshanas, a word that means seeing: Nyaya on how you know, Vaisheshika on what there is, Samkhya and Yoga on the witness and the stilled mind, Mimamsa on the rites, Vedanta on what is real. Their teachers argued for centuries, and many teachers treat honest debate, shastrartha, as a way of serving the truth. The Rig Veda put it early: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. So one family can hold a father who lives by the rites and a grandmother who lives by knowing, under one roof, and both are inside the tradition. The path doesn't crown a winner. It asks you to argue the way Ubhaya Bharati judged: fairly, and with flowers on.
screen: `MIMAMSA VERSUS VEDANTA.` · `THE JUDGE: UBHAYA BHARATI.` · `MANDANA BECOMES A STUDENT.` · `DARSHANA: A WAY OF SEEING.` · then, large: `TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT BY MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose view of God or religion differs from yours, at home or at work. Picture a fresh garland around their neck and around yours, and say their view to yourself in its strongest, fairest form before you say your own. If you pray, ask to see the truth more clearly, whoever's flowers fade first.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the darshanas, Hinduism's schools of thought, argued hard and never ranked. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Even a debate can be held with flowers on. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1417.title: Rantideva's last cup of water
1417.hook: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast, and the guests keep coming
1417.carry: seva: work offered, its fruit given away
1417.tomorrow: rain, a tiny shelter, three strangers, and then a fourth.
1417.howItsDone: Hindus practice seva in many forms: cooking and serving food at temples, caring for the sick and elderly, or working in the community, offered as service to God rather than for reward.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shankara and Mandana Mishra argued the schools of thought, with a garland for a judge: truth is one, the wise give it many names.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `TRUTH IS ONE, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: The plate is finally in front of him. King Rantideva and his family have gone without food for a long time, and now there's a little rice, a little ghee, some water. He lifts his hand to eat. A knock. A hungry guest. The king shares. Another knock, another guest. He shares again. Then a man arrives with his dogs, all of them hungry. Today's summit sit climbs back to the lineage track, and the stretch on karma and seva: work, and work given away.
screen: `THE PLATE, FINALLY.` → `A KNOCK. ANOTHER KNOCK.` → `WORK, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Bhagavata finishes the story, in paraphrase. The king gives the man with the dogs everything that's left, and bows to him and to the dogs. Only the water remains. Then one more person comes, an outcaste by the rules of the day, thirsty, asking for a drink. The king gives him the water and says something. He doesn't want great powers from God, he says, and doesn't even ask to be freed from rebirth. He asks to enter the sorrow of all beings and carry it, so they can be free of it. Then the story turns: the guests were gods come to test him. They show themselves, and he asks them for nothing. Hold that next to the rest of the track. In the Uddhava Gita, a wandering beggar has his bowl snatched away, and he blames no one, not people, not the gods, not even karma, only the grip of his own mind. In the Gita, Krishna says the true renouncer isn't the one who quits his work and lets the fire go out, but the one who does the needed work without leaning on what it brings back. And seva: service, offered as worship. Karma isn't just a ledger of what comes back to you. It's work done without clutching the result, and seva is that work when the result goes to someone else. Rantideva's meal fed a guest, a stranger, a man with dogs and a thirsty outcaste, and when the gods stood before him, he had nothing left to ask for. It's why many Hindu temples cook and serve free meals and call it seva.
screen: `THE LAST OF THE WATER, GIVEN.` · `THE BOWL SNATCHED, NO ONE BLAMED.` · `DO THE WORK, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · `SEVA: WORK WHOSE FRUIT GOES TO ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOTHING LEFT TO ASK FOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary piece of work you'll do today, a shift, a meal, a report, a ride for someone. On an out-breath, let your shoulders drop as if setting down what it will bring you, the thanks, the credit, the result; keep the work, let the fruit go, and if you pray, offer the work to God before you begin.

segments.voice: Your line: seva is work offered to God, its fruit given away. The work stays in your hands. Rest well.

1418.title: Three poets in a crowded shelter
1418.hook: rain, a dark narrow shelter, three strangers pressed together, and then a fourth who wasn't there before
1418.carry: bhakti: love for god is its own fruit
1418.tomorrow: a glint in the wet sand. silver, or only a shell?
1418.howItsDone: The hymns of the Alvars are sung in Sri Vaishnava temples and homes in Tamil Nadu, and the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied and recited by devotees of many bhakti traditions.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva: work offered, its fruit given away, and a king who gave away his last cup of water.
screen: `SEVA: WORK OFFERED, FRUIT GIVEN.` · `THE LAST CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Rain is coming down hard at night. A wandering devotee ducks into a tiny shelter by a house. A second traveler knocks, and the first makes room. A third arrives, soaked, and the two make room again, and now they stand shoulder to shoulder. And then, tradition says, they feel a fourth pressing in among them, someone none of them can see. That's the story told of the first Alvars, the Tamil singers of Vishnu. Today's summit sit climbs back to the bhakti stretch, and the lamps those three lit.
screen: `RAIN, AND A TINY SHELTER.` → `ROOM MADE, AND MADE AGAIN.` → `A FOURTH, PRESSING IN.`

segments.voice: In the story, each sings a verse to light the dark. The first, Poygai, makes a lamp of the world: the earth for its bowl, the ocean for its oil, the sun for its flame. The second, Bhutam, makes a lamp of the heart: love for the bowl, longing for the oil, a melting mind for the wick. And the third, Pey, by that light, says simply: I have seen. The Lord is there, with the goddess, in the crowded dark. Now hold that next to the Narada Bhakti Sutras, the short book the year read whole. Its boldest claim is that bhakti, love for God, isn't the road to something else. It is where the road goes. Love is its own fruit. And when the sutras try to say what that love is like, they give up gracefully: it can't be told, like a taste in the mouth of someone who can't speak. You can have it. You can't hand it over in words. From up here, the shelter and the sutras say one thing in two keys. The singers don't argue their way to God. They light lamps and look, and the lamps are made of what they already have: the whole world, for one, their own love, for another. Then think of the women of the bhakti stretch, and the singers of the regions: a tailor, a cobbler, a weaver, singing to God in a home language. The shelter was too small. They made room anyway. And that, the story says, is when God pressed in.
screen: `A LAMP MADE OF THE WORLD.` · `A LAMP MADE OF LOVE.` · `LOVE IS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `A TASTE THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.` · then, large: `THEY MADE ROOM ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Notice how full the mind is, the way the shelter was full, and without pushing anything out, make a little room on each out-breath, the way the first traveler shifted over for the second. If you pray, let that room be for God, as the Alvars felt someone press in; if you don't, let it be room for whoever comes next today.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: bhakti, the Alvars' lamps in a crowded shelter, and a love the sutras call its own fruit. Today's word.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti, love for God, is its own fruit. A small shelter, and still room for one more. Until tomorrow.

1419.howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta study the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher, and pair the study with reflection and meditation on what the self is.

segments.voice: Low tide, late afternoon. Something in the wet sand catches the sun and flashes, bright as a dropped coin. It's a shell. Nothing about the shell changed when it was picked up. It was a shell the whole time. What changed was the seeing. Shankara chose very nearly this picture to open his commentary on the Brahma Sutras. Today's summit sit climbs back to the last stretch of the lineage track: jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A GLINT IN THE SAND.` → `ONLY A SHELL.` → `THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Before he comments on a single line of the Brahma Sutras, Shankara writes a preface about that shell: mother-of-pearl taken for silver, one thing mistaken for another. His teaching is that a mistake like this sits at the root of bondage: taking the body and the mind, which come and go, for the self, the atman, which doesn't. Gaudapada, in his verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, gives the same kind of picture. On a dim path, a rope is taken for a snake. The fear is real. The snake isn't. What ends the fear isn't fighting the snake or running from it. It's seeing. When the rope is seen as rope, the snake doesn't leave. It was never there. The Brahma Sutras themselves open with a word that sounds almost casual: now. Now, then, the wish to know Brahman. In his comment on the fourth sutra, Shankara says freedom isn't produced, the way a pot is made from clay. It's what is already so, uncovered, the way the shell was always a shell. Gaudapada's last picture is a firebrand whirled in the dark, drawing circles that aren't there. Hold the stick still, and the circles stop. From up here, jnana looks less like piling up information and more like a light coming on. Ramanuja, whom the year also read, reads it differently: he holds the world and the selves in it as real, the body of God, not a mistake to be seen through. But on the jnana track, the work is this: a bad grade, a mood, a hard week pass across you the way the snake passed across the rope. They aren't you. Look closely enough, and what frightened you turns out to be rope.
screen: `THE SHELL TAKEN FOR SILVER.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `NOW, THEN, THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THE FIREBRAND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `IT WAS ALWAYS ROPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one worry that has been coiled on your path lately, and instead of fighting it, look at it more closely, the way a flashlight would: what exactly is there, and what have you added in the dim light? Stay with plain seeing for a while, then let the worry rest and rest as the one who sees; if you pray, ask for clear sight.

1420.title: Ushas, the dawn who wakes the world
1420.hook: the sky going pale over a parking lot, and a Vedic singer who saw the same light and gave it a name
1420.carry: the vedas still greet every dawn
1420.tomorrow: the ocean is churned, and a healer rises holding a pot.
1420.howItsDone: Vedic hymns are recited from memory in traditional schools of chanting, and Hindus who keep a morning practice may greet the day with prayers such as the Gayatri, often facing the rising sun.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rope that was only ever rope. Jnana: you are the atman, not the passing mind.
screen: `JNANA: YOU ARE THE ATMAN.` · `IT WAS ALWAYS ROPE.`

segments.voice: Early, before the alarm. Out the window, the sky over the parking lot goes from black to gray to something like the inside of a peach. A bird starts, then another. Nobody will write a hymn about this morning. But weeks of this year went into hymns that did exactly that, sung to the fire, to the storm, to the dark before creation, and to this light. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Vedas themselves, and to Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `BLACK, GRAY, PEACH.` → `A BIRD, THEN ANOTHER.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, the dawn is a goddess, and the singers talk to her like someone they know. In one hymn, in paraphrase, she wakes every living thing and sends each off to its own work: one to look for food, one to its task, one to its prayer. She travels the same path every morning, never wearing out. The people who watched the dawns before us are gone, the hymn says. We are the ones seeing her now, and others will come after us who will see her too. From up here, look how much of the Vedas stretch was like that. The very first hymn of the Rig Veda calls on Agni, the fire. Vasishtha asks Varuna why their friendship went cold. A hymn quotes, out loud, the people who doubt Indra exists. The hymn of creation ends with or perhaps not. The Atharva Veda sits at a sickbed with a glass of water. And the Gayatri turns out to be a verse to Savitr, the sun as the one who sets things moving. The year found that the Vedas aren't only ancient rules. They are people talking to the world as if it could hear: the fire, the water, the dark and the morning. And they aren't only old. In many Hindu homes, someone still greets the sunrise the way the singers did, with the morning prayer called sandhya and the Gayatri: may we meditate on the light of Savitr; may it stir our minds. Ushas arrives every day. The hymn says we are the ones seeing her now.
screen: `THE DAWN WAKES EVERY LIVING THING.` · `THOSE BEFORE US, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `FIRE, VARUNA, DOUBT, A SICKBED.` · `SANDHYA: THE GAYATRI AT SUNRISE.` · then, large: `SHE ARRIVES EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Look at the light in a window, whatever the hour, or remember the last sunrise you saw. Bring to mind those who watched dawns before you, a grandparent, someone gone, and those who will see dawns after you, and sit in the middle of that line; if you pray, greet the dawn as the singers did. If missing someone weighs heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

1421.title: Dhanvantari rises with the nectar
1421.hook: the gods and demons churn the ocean, and a healer rises holding the pot of nectar

1421.howItsDone: Many Hindu families honor Dhanvantari on Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, with lamps and prayers for health; some also draw on Ayurvedic ideas, such as a morning routine or seasonal eating, alongside modern medicine.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the Vedas still greet every dawn, with Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing.
screen: `THE VEDAS STILL GREET EVERY DAWN.` · `THE DAWN, BEFORE THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: The ocean of milk is being churned. The gods pull one end of a great serpent wound around a mountain, the demons pull the other, and the sea foams and foams. Poison comes up first, and Shiva drinks it. And then, out of the white water, a figure rises, dark and shining, holding a pot. It's Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, and the pot holds amrita, the nectar. Today's summit sit climbs back to Ayurveda, and the god many Hindus pray to for health.
screen: `THE OCEAN, CHURNED.` → `A HEALER RISES.` → `A POT OF NECTAR.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, Dhanvantari is a part of Vishnu himself, and the one who brings Ayurveda, the science of long life. Many families honor him on Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, with a lamp and a prayer for health. Here's the teaching Hindus take from him: caring for the body isn't vanity, and it isn't separate from religion. The poet Kalidasa put it in a line people still quote: the body is the first tool of dharma. The Charaka Samhita says it plainly: health is the root of the four aims of a life, dharma, a good living, love, and freedom. This year we read Ayurveda's doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, like weather: a way of noticing, not a diagnosis; nothing here replaces a doctor. The classical daily round cleans the teeth and the tongue, keeps exercise to about half your strength, and Charaka's good conduct says to greet people first. Patanjali asks for breath long and subtle, not forced. And the Sushruta Samhita's definition of the healthy person lists a body in balance, then doesn't stop: it ends with a self, senses and mind that are clear and content. The word for healthy, svastha, can be read as standing in yourself. So when a Hindu grandmother says eat, sleep, go for a walk, she isn't only fussing. In this tradition, the body is where prayer, work and love happen, and tending it is part of the climb.
screen: `DHANVANTARI: PHYSICIAN OF THE GODS.` · `THE BODY: DHARMA'S FIRST TOOL.` · `DOSHAS: NOTICING, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.` · `A MIND CLEAR AND CONTENT.` · then, large: `SVASTHA: STANDING IN YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath as it is, without changing anything, then let the out-breath grow a little longer and quieter, long and subtle, not big and loud, letting it go back to normal if it strains. At the end, ask the old question gently: are the senses at ease, is the mind content, even a little? Don't fix anything; just notice. If you pray, offer a short prayer for the health of someone you love, as families do on Dhanteras.
